document: Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act
text: Device qualification starts with intended use: diagnosis of disease or other conditions, cure, mitigation, treatment or prevention of disease, or affecting the structure or function of the body. The statutory definition expressly accounts for software functions excluded under section 520(o). Apply the definition to each software function, not merely the product platform.

document: Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act
text: Section 520(o)(1) excludes specified software functions from the device definition, including certain administrative support, healthy-lifestyle, electronic record, transfer/store/format/display, and clinical decision support functions. Each exclusion has conditions and must be assessed at the function level.

document: Policy for Device Software Functions and Mobile Medical Applications
text: FDA applies a risk-based, function-specific policy to software functions that meet the device definition. The policy is independent of whether a function runs on a mobile platform, general-purpose computer, or within or as part of a hardware device. It distinguishes non-device functions, device functions under enforcement discretion, and device functions that are the focus of oversight.

document: Clinical Decision Support Software
text: FDA's CDS guidance explains four statutory criteria for Non-Device CDS. Screening includes whether the function analyzes medical images or signals, displays or analyzes medical information, supports or provides recommendations to a health care professional, and enables that professional to independently review the basis so they do not rely primarily on the recommendation. Patient/caregiver functions do not satisfy the HCP-only criterion.

document: General Wellness: Policy for Low Risk Devices
text: FDA's general-wellness policy addresses products intended only for general wellness use that present low risk. Healthy-lifestyle software unrelated to diagnosis, cure, mitigation, prevention, or treatment may also fall within the statutory software exclusion. The 2026 guidance supersedes the 2019 version and should be consulted for current examples and risk factors.

document: Medical Device Data Systems, Medical Image Storage Devices, and Medical Image Communications Devices
text: A data function that is solely intended to transfer, store, convert formats, or display medical-device data or results may be a Non-Device-MDDS function under section 520(o)(1)(D). Analysis, interpretation, active monitoring, device control, or generation of alarms can take a function outside that data-only screening path.

document: Content of Premarket Submissions for Device Software Functions
section: Recommended documentation for device software functions
text: For device software functions in premarket submissions, FDA recommends risk-based basic or enhanced documentation. Recommended content covers items such as level-of-concern rationale, software description, risk management, architecture, requirements, design, development and configuration practices, testing, version history, unresolved anomalies, and revision-level history as applicable.

document: Off-The-Shelf Software Use in Medical Devices
section: OTS software information and hazard analysis
text: FDA's OTS guidance addresses information needed to evaluate generally available software used in a medical device. Screening should consider the OTS component's intended role, known anomalies, hazard and risk controls, configuration, maintenance, continued support, and the evidence needed for a premarket submission.

document: Cybersecurity in Medical Devices: Quality Management System Considerations and Content of Premarket Submissions
section: Secure product development framework and premarket documentation
text: FDA recommends integrating cybersecurity into the device quality system and total product lifecycle. For cybersecurity-relevant device software, assess threat modeling, security architecture, risk controls, testing, vulnerability management, update capability, labeling, and required premarket information. The February 2026 revision aligns terminology with the QMSR and supersedes the June 2025 version.

document: Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Device Software Functions: Lifecycle Management and Marketing Submission Recommendations
text: FDA's draft AI-enabled device software guidance presents total-product-lifecycle recommendations for design, development, documentation, performance, transparency, bias considerations, postmarket monitoring, and change management. Because it is draft guidance, the navigator must label it non-final and must not present its recommendations as binding requirements.

document: Marketing Submission Recommendations for a Predetermined Change Control Plan for Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Device Software Functions
section: PCCP description, modification protocol, and impact assessment
text: A PCCP may prospectively describe certain planned modifications to an AI-enabled device software function, the protocol for developing, validating, and implementing those modifications, and an assessment of their impact. A PCCP is relevant only when post-authorization changes are planned; AI use alone does not mean a PCCP is mandatory.

document: Quality Management System Regulation
text: The Quality Management System Regulation in 21 CFR Part 820 became effective February 2, 2026. It incorporates ISO 13485:2016 by reference with FDA-specific provisions. Device manufacturers must determine the applicable quality-system processes; software used in production or the quality system may require controlled, risk-based validation even when that software is not itself a medical device.

status: Edition 1.1; verify recognition and local adoption
section: Scope; lifecycle processes; software safety classification
text: IEC 62304 provides lifecycle-process requirements for medical-device software, whether software is itself a medical device or is embedded in or integral to a device. Its process structure covers development, maintenance, software risk management, configuration management, and problem resolution. Preliminary safety classes A, B, and C correspond to increasing potential harm, subject to the standard's detailed classification logic and risk-control architecture. Consult a licensed copy for clause-level requirements.

status: Current edition; verify amendments, recognition, and local adoption
text: ISO 14971 defines a lifecycle process for identifying medical-device hazards, estimating and evaluating associated risks, controlling risks, and monitoring control effectiveness. Software contributions to hazardous situations should connect software requirements, architecture, verification, and residual-risk evaluation to the device risk-management file. Consult a licensed copy for normative clauses.

document: Software as a Medical Device (SaMD): Key Definitions
status: Final; harmonized framework, not a jurisdictional regulation
text: IMDRF defines SaMD as software intended for one or more medical purposes that performs those purposes without being part of a hardware medical device. Software that drives or is required by a hardware medical device does not meet that SaMD definition, although it can remain regulated device software under a jurisdiction's framework.

document: Software as a Medical Device: Possible Framework for Risk Categorization and Corresponding Considerations
status: Final; harmonized framework, not a jurisdictional regulation
topics: SaMD category I II III IV
text: The N12 framework combines the significance of information provided by SaMD—treat or diagnose, drive clinical management, or inform clinical management—with the critical, serious, or non-serious state of the health-care situation or condition. The resulting relative-impact categories run from I (lowest) through IV (highest). These IMDRF categories are not the same as FDA device class or EU MDR class.

document: Software as a Medical Device (SaMD): Application of Quality Management System
status: Final; harmonized framework, not a jurisdictional regulation
text: IMDRF N23 describes quality-management principles tailored to SaMD, including governance, scalable lifecycle activities, product planning, development, verification and validation, deployment, maintenance, and monitoring. It is a harmonized technical framework, not a substitute for the binding requirements of a particular jurisdiction.

document: Software as a Medical Device (SaMD): Clinical Evaluation
status: Final; harmonized framework, not a jurisdictional regulation
section: Valid clinical association, analytical validation, clinical validation
text: IMDRF N41 frames SaMD clinical evaluation around valid clinical association, analytical or technical validation, and clinical validation. The level and type of evidence should be appropriate to the SaMD's intended purpose and risk. This harmonized framework does not itself create jurisdiction-specific legal requirements.

document: Regulation (EU) 2017/745 on medical devices
status: Consolidated text available; authenticate against Official Journal
section: Article 2(1) device definition and Article 2(12) intended purpose
text: EU MDR qualification turns on the manufacturer's intended purpose and whether software has a medical purpose within the device definition. General-purpose software used in health care is not automatically a medical device. Qualification must precede classification.

document: Regulation (EU) 2017/745 on medical devices
status: Consolidated text available; authenticate against Official Journal
text: Rule 11 classifies software that supplies information used for diagnostic or therapeutic decisions as class IIa, with class IIb or III escalation where an incorrect decision can cause serious deterioration, surgical intervention, death, or irreversible deterioration. Software monitoring physiological processes is generally IIa, escalating to IIb for vital parameters where variations could create immediate danger. Other software is class I, subject to all MDR implementing rules.

document: Regulation (EU) 2017/745 on medical devices
status: Consolidated text available; authenticate against Official Journal
section: Annex I, General Safety and Performance Requirements
text: Medical Device Software must satisfy applicable Annex I general safety and performance requirements. Relevant themes include risk management, repeatability and reliability, software lifecycle and state of the art, verification and validation, information security, and protection against unauthorized access. Applicability should be documented in the technical documentation rather than inferred solely from class.
